checkpoints: A `queued` status from an SMS provider's send call only confirms the provider accepted the request into its own pipeline — it says nothing about whether the carrier actually delivered the message to the phone, since the real `sent → delivered/failed` outcome is decided later, out of band from the `create()` response.

A fixed-delay timer that resends an OTP whenever it fires, without checking delivery outcome, is a blind guess standing in for missing information: because most users read and type a code slower than the provider needs to deliver it, the timer routinely fires after the first message already arrived, producing a paid duplicate send on nearly every successful login.

When a message is genuinely failing (for example, carrier filtering on the sender ID), retrying it identically down the same route just pays for more guaranteed failures instead of solving the underlying delivery problem.

Registering the provider's status-callback webhook lets delivery state be pushed asynchronously as the message transitions `queued → sent → delivered/failed`; persisting that status per message (keyed by the provider's message id) gives the system a ground truth to react to instead of a clock.

Automatic resend should be driven exclusively by an observed `failed`/`undelivered` status from the webhook, never by elapsed time — this eliminates the duplicate-spend pattern because a message already marked delivered is never resent.

A user-visible "resend code" action needs to be separated from automatic delivery-failure resend and gated by its own cooldown window plus a persistent attempt cap, so that repeated manual taps still result in at most one real paid send once the cooldown clears.

After repeated delivery failures on the same route, the system should escalate laterally to a fallback — an alternate SMS route/regional provider, or a different channel such as email — rather than retrying the identical send a third time down a route that has already proven broken.

Keeping one idempotency key per logical send intent ensures that infrastructure-level retries (crashed workers, retried jobs) can never trigger a second paid send for what is conceptually the same OTP attempt.

Moving from a fixed timer to webhook-driven resend trades a small amount of latency (waiting on the provider's real signal) and added infrastructure (a callback endpoint and its own reliability) for near-elimination of duplicate spend — an acceptable trade for a channel that bills per message sent.

Correct behavior can be validated by simulating provider callbacks: a `delivered` callback should trigger no resend, a `failed` callback should trigger exactly one resend, and rapidly repeated clicks on the user-triggered resend endpoint should still be constrained by the cooldown and attempt cap.
